First, I agree with you 100% on eliminating noncompetes. But we shouldn’t overstate what that alone can accomplish.

Freedom to leave matters. So does having somewhere viable to go. When a few hospital systems dominate a market, eliminating noncompetes alone won’t restore meaningful competition or make independent practice financially viable.

California has long prohibited most employment noncompetes, yet healthcare consolidation has continued.

If we simultaneously create regulations that make independent practices harder to finance, build, and sustain, we undermine the alternatives that give physicians real bargaining power. Eliminating noncompetes needs to go hand in hand with protecting those alternatives.

Despite what @DGlaucomflecken implies…

MSOs are used by private equity AND by independent physicians. For independent practices, they allow practices to pool resources, share administrative services and reduce overhead. This is critical for many independent practices in the current environment. 

No, the bill doesn’t ban MSOs outright. 
But, It does restrict their contracts and management relationships, with no blanket exemption for physician owned MSOs. Requirements for independent advisers and fair market value compensation add compliance obligations.

Meanwhile, hospitals and hospital affiliated clinics are exempt from the core ownership prohibition.  Honestly, they are exempt from many of the regulations that apply to physicians.

To be clear, I don’t have an issue with people who object to private equity owning medical  practices.

My objection is to leveraging the corporate boogie man to restrict a tool physicians also use to remain independent while preserving the hospital ownership pathway.

The predictable consequence is more legal expense, more compliance risk and greater difficulty operating an independent practice. That gives hospitals another competitive advantage, packaged as protection for physician independence.

I would love their thoughts

Here is a littlbit of context on the issues with Warren’s proposed bill.  Remember, it has to do with how regulator will interpret the language and potentially write the regulations to implement the law 

Which will determine how far the MSO restrictions reach into physician groups with no private equity involvement.

But let’s look at the actual language:

Section 2(d)(4) defines an MSO by the services it provides. Billing, payroll, IT, scheduling, leasing. Nothing in that definition requires private equity or outside investors.
Section 2(b)(2) applies the restrictions to the MSO and its “shareholder, director, member, manager, officer, employee, or contractor.” There is no explicit exemption because those people happen to be physicians.
Those same people would be restricted from owning, working for or managing a medical practice. Read literally, physicians who own both their practice and a shared MSO could have an ownership problem. That language needs clarification.
Management agreements require negotiations “at arm’s length” through independently selected advisers without financial conflicts with the MSO. Fees must reflect “fair market value” as determined by the FTC. This includes amendments, renewals and terminations.
The restrictions reach ultimate control over staffing, compensation, billing, pricing and payer contracts when that control affects the nature or quality of care. Those are significant parts of running a practice. Bill text

So physicians trying to pool resources could have to reassess ownership, revise agreements, support their management fees and potentially restructure their businesses.

That means more legal expense and uncertainty for independent groups trying to work together and grow. Having physicians own the MSO does not automatically protect them from these requirements.
